issues.issue: The Subscriber "approves the provision of such services" after being "informed" of them "and of the fees payable," without identifying the services, the affiliates, or any fee figure, so the scope of the approval is indeterminate.
This approval of Trustee investment management services is hard to square with Section 5(a)'s representation that the Subscriber "is not relying on a financial advisor" in acquiring Shares.

The clause is conditional ("in the event that any assets of an employee benefit plan may be invested") yet states an unconditional fiduciary status, and the unclosed quotation around "ERISA" obscures where the definition ends.

Automatic reaffirmation on each additional contribution interacts awkwardly with Section 4, under which contributions occur whenever collateral is received under the separate securities lending agreement, so reaffirmation may occur without any deliberate act.
The notice duty is triggered whenever representations "shall not be true and correct" but fixes no time for giving notice and no consequence for failure.

The indemnity runs to "each Affiliate" of the Trust and Trustee, a capitalized term defined only in the unattached Declaration of Trust, and covers "any and all loss, damage or liability due or arising out of" a breach without any causation or limitation language.
An indemnity in favor of the Trustee sits against Section 12, which says the obligations created shall not be binding upon the Trustee and that all persons shall look solely to Trust assets.
Conditions must be fulfilled "to the Trust's satisfaction" while this condition also requires the representations to be true "in all material respects," mixing a subjective and an objective standard.

The condition assumes cash raised under the securities lending agreement pays the "purchase price," whereas Section 4 requires a contribution of cash, securities or other property equal to collateral received, so the payment mechanic is described twice and differently.

"Such other information and ... certifications or other documents" as the Trust "reasonably shall have requested, including with respect to" securities-law compliance leaves the catch-all's reach against the named example uncertain.
The Agreement is "governed by the State of Minnesota" rather than by its laws, and the phrase "and any applicable Federal law" is added without saying how the two interact.
Minnesota governing law must be reconciled with the Declaration of Trust incorporated by Sections 1 and 3, a Maryland business trust instrument whose terms bind the Subscriber as a Shareholder.

The entire-agreement clause conflicts with Section 5(b), which recites reliance on the Confidential Memorandum and "any additional documents" furnished by the Trustee, and with Section 3, which binds the Subscriber to the Declaration of Trust.
Binding effect extends only to "heirs and legal representatives," omitting successors and assigns, which for an institutional Subscriber is an odd and arguably inoperative list.
The clause says headings shall not affect the "interpretation or affect" of any term, an evident misuse of "affect" for "effect."
This permits modification by a writing signed only by the party against whom it is enforced, while Section 9(b) permits amendment "only by a writing executed by the Subscriber and the Trust."

A flat bar on assignment by the Subscriber sits against Section 9(b), which makes the Agreement binding on the Subscriber's "heirs and legal representatives," and against Section 5(h) contemplating Trustee-consented transfers of Shares.

Survival of all Subscriber rights and obligations through dissolution is difficult to reconcile with Section 9(e)'s bar on any transfer or assignment, since a dissolved entity's rights can pass only by transfer.

Acceptance is said to be in the Trustee's sole discretion but effective "only upon execution and delivery ... by the Trust," which does not match Section 2's statement that acceptance or rejection is the Trustee's, nor Section 3's acceptance "by the Trustee on behalf of the Trust."
Notice is "deemed given when personally delivered or mailed" to the address "set forth below," but the signature page leaves the notice fax line and duplicate-statement fields blank.

"The obligation created thereby" is unclear as to whose obligations are limited, and the closing phrase "any claim arising in connection therein" is garbled, leaving the scope of the exculpation open.

The statement that obligations are not binding on the Trustee conflicts with the preamble, in which Wells Fargo Bank, N.A. as Trustee is a contracting party, and with Section 7's indemnity running to the Trustee.
The sentence is incomplete — it ends at "or faxed to" with no number — and uses the permissive "should" rather than a mandatory notice requirement.

This states an unqualified non-liability for unauthorized or fraudulent telephone instructions, while the Authorizations paragraph limits non-liability to requests "believed by it to be genuine and in accordance with the procedures described in the Trust's Confidential Memorandum."
The authority runs to "persons indicated above," but the Authorized Personnel table on the executed form is blank, leaving no identified persons.
The authorizations continue "until written notice is provided," without saying what the notice must say, when it takes effect, or who may give it.

The proviso is incomplete and unintelligible as written — "so long as, in the case of redemption, CL by the Trust or Wells Fargo to the account(s) designated above" has no verb — so the condition on the liability limitation cannot be applied.

The good-faith-belief limitation cannot be squared with the preceding Subscriber Information paragraph stating flatly that neither the Trust nor Wells Fargo will be liable for any unauthorized or fraudulent telephone instructions.
